source: Fu, Wang, Tian, Zhao (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Gap 1. On long-chain reasoning models, an online rule that stops sampling when the weighted vote share reaches 0.95 (or a budget cap K=512) cut tokens by 18 to 85 percent versus full majority voting at the same cap. The confidence-filtered variants (top 10 percent traces) often raised accuracy too.
numbers: Budget K=512, 64 resampled runs, models DeepSeek-8B, Qwen3-32B, GPT-OSS-120B, 4 math sets. DeepConf-low token cut 43-84.7 percent (GPT-OSS-120B AIME25: 97.1 to 97.9 percent accuracy, -84.7 percent tokens; DeepSeek-8B AIME24: 86.7 to 92.5, -77.9). DeepConf-high cut 18-59 percent with accuracy within about 1 point. Offline AIME25 GPT-OSS-120B: 97.0 majority vs 99.9 filtered.
quote: relying on very few traces risks incorrect answers if the model exhibits bias
limits: Needs token log-probs and a 16-trace warmup to set the threshold. Savings only start after the 16 warmup traces, so they are larger at K=512 than at K=32 (52.8 vs 15.4 percent at 0.95 for the low variant). Accuracy dropped on some sets: Qwen3-8B AIME25 -4.4 points; Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9; GPT-OSS-120B HMMT25 filtering hurt. Table row labels are scrambled in the PDF text; the AIME25 label for the 84.7 percent cell follows the paper intro.
agent_relevance: Yes for gap 1: an agreement bound at 0.95 does survive on open reasoning models with long chains, but it needs a minimum sample count first (16) and savings depend on a high cap.

source: Fu et al. (2025) DeepConf, Appendix B.1 consensus threshold ablation and limitations
finding: Gap 1 and 2. The stop threshold on agreement is a real knob. 0.95 kept accuracy exactly and 1.0 saved less. Looser bounds (0.90, 0.85) saved up to 69.6 percent tokens but cost accuracy in the aggressive filter variant. The authors name model overconfidence on wrong answers as the main limitation.
numbers: Qwen3-32B, AIME24. At bound 0.95: tokens -15.4 percent (B=32) and -52.8 percent (B=512) for DeepConf-low, -22.0 and -54.7 for DeepConf-high, accuracy delta 0. At 0.90: DeepConf-low -0.26 points accuracy. DeepConf-high held full accuracy even at 0.85.
quote: addressing cases where models exhibit high confidence on incorrect reasoning paths
limits: One model and one dataset for the threshold ablation. No count of how many stops landed on a wrong consensus.
agent_relevance: Supports a bound near 0.95 as the default; a looser bound is safe only when low-quality traces are also filtered. Confident-wrong remains named but unmeasured.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Gap 4 and 2. Coverage (any sample right, i.e. a perfect verifier) climbs over orders of magnitude of samples, but majority vote and a reward model plateau near 100 samples. Many problems have a correct answer that is sampled rarely, so the consensus answer is wrong.
numbers: Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH: coverage 82.9 percent at 100 samples to 98.44 percent at 10,000; majority vote or reward model only 40.50 to 41.41 percent over the same range. SWE-bench Lite DeepSeek-Coder-V2: 15.9 percent at 1 sample to 56 percent at 250 (single-sample SOTA 43). 11.3 percent of SWE-bench Lite problems have flaky tests.
quote: these increasingly rare correct generations are only beneficial if verifiers can find the needle in the haystack
limits: Open-weight small models, 2024. Equal-sample comparison, not equal tokens. The reward model was ArmoRM-Llama3-8B.
agent_relevance: A verifier bound (tests pass) can keep paying off to thousands of samples; an agreement bound cannot (it stops improving near 100). Where a verifier exists, stop on the verifier, not on agreement.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2024, v3 2026) Inference scaling flaws: the limits of LLM resampling with imperfect verifiers
finding: Gap 4. A verifier bound is not free of failure: unit tests miss errors, so the false-positive rate rises with the number of attempts K. With a cost for a false positive the best number of attempts is often below 10 and can be zero.
numbers: HumanEval+ and MBPP, several open models. At cost-to-benefit ratio 4 the optimal K is about 5 for all four models in the figure. Single-sample accuracy correlates strongly with false-positive rate. Llama-3.1-70B false-positive rate rises steeply with K; Code Llama and Command families rise gradually.
quote: weaker models cannot sample their way to top-level performance
limits: Code only; the check is the benchmark's own test suite vs a stricter extended suite. Authors could not explain why model families differ.
agent_relevance: Cap the verifier bound too. A test-pass stop on weak tests is a confident-wrong source; use stronger or independent checks and a small K cap.

source: Zhao, Awasthi, Gollapudi (2025) Sample, Scrutinize and Scale: inference-time search by scaling verification
finding: Gap 4. At 200 samples, picking by the model's own repeated verification beat picking by agreement on every benchmark; consistency stalled when 200 became 1,000. Agreement fails when the right answer is rare (an AIME problem where 1 of 200 samples was correct).
numbers: Gemini v1.5 Pro, 200 samples, 50 verification scores per sample. AIME (15 items): pass@1 1, Consistency@200 4, Consistency@1000 3, Verification@200 8, o1-Preview 7. MATH (500): 426, 460, 460, 467, 428. LiveBench Math (200): 104, 118, 120, 135, 131. LiveBench Reasoning (140): 63, 75, 73, 97, 95.
quote: Consistency@k stagnates on AIME and LiveBench Reasoning.
limits: Verification costs 50 extra scores per sample, so this is NOT equal tokens. Small AIME set (15). Authors say frontier models show weak out-of-box verification.
agent_relevance: Verifier-based selection beat agreement at equal sample count by 7 to 22 items (MATH +7 of 500), but costs far more tokens per sample. The equal-token head-to-head is still missing.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Gap 3 and 5. The best way to spend test-time compute depends on question difficulty. Easy questions: sequential revision or more sampling pays. Hard questions: tree search beats best-of-N. A per-difficulty strategy matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute. Difficulty bins from the model's own pass rate predicted gains better than hand-labelled MATH levels.
numbers: PaLM 2-S* on MATH. Compute-optimal scaling can outperform best-of-N using up to 4x less test-time compute; in some regimes a smaller model plus test-time compute beats a 14x larger model. Beam search beats best-of-N on levels 3 and 4 only.
quote: question difficulty acts as a sufficient statistic of a question when designing the compute-optimal strategy
limits: Main analysis uses difficulty bins computed from many samples per question; a cheap estimator is a separate approximation. MATH only.
agent_relevance: Supports a difficulty-dependent bound (not one fixed number) but the difficulty estimate costs samples. Model-based pass-rate bins beat human labels.

source: Chen, Davis, Hanin et al. (2024) Are more LM calls all you need? Towards scaling laws of compound inference systems
finding: Gap 3. With mixed difficulty, majority-vote accuracy can first rise and then fall as the number of calls grows. More calls help easy queries and hurt hard queries (where the right answer is the minority). Theory plus experiments give a way to estimate the best number of calls from a small sample.
numbers: Non-monotone curves shown on MMLU Physics, TruthfulQA, GPQA, AVeriTeC (Vote and Filter-Vote). A query is easy if the model gets it right with probability above 0.5.
quote: more LM calls lead to higher performance on easy queries, but lower performance on hard queries
limits: Fixed-N voting analysis, not a sequential stop rule. Models are 2024 GPT-class.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a capped bound: on hard items extra samples make the confident-wrong answer MORE likely to win. A single fixed bound across mixed items is not neutral; cap it or set it per item.

source: Chen, Xu, Liang et al. (2024/2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Gap 1 and 3. Reasoning models spend MORE solution rounds on easy problems, and later rounds add little. A self-training fix shortens output without lowering accuracy. This is the opposite of a bound that collapses with difficulty.
numbers: QwQ-32B-Preview produces 2 to 4 solution rounds in 76 to 80 percent of cases (DeepSeek-R1: 59 to 63 percent); easier test sets get more rounds.
limits: Counts rounds inside one chain, not across samples. Efficiency numbers are model-specific.
agent_relevance: Long chains already contain internal re-checks; a stop rule across samples must be priced against that internal repetition.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Gap 8 (closest proxy) and 1. A token-level bound can be moved on command: forcing the end-of-thinking token ends thinking early, appending 'Wait' makes the model continue. More thinking lifted AIME24 from 50 to 57 percent; parallel majority voting on the base model did not catch up.
numbers: s1-32B on AIME24: 50 percent to 57 percent with budget forcing (ignoring end-of-thinking 2x/4x/6x and appending Wait). 'Wait' worked best of the strings tried.
limits: Not a speed-vs-accuracy instruction; it changes the stop token. One fine-tuned model; gains flatten at larger forced lengths. No accuracy-per-token rate reported.
agent_relevance: A hard stop and a forced continue are both cheap bound controls in a reasoning model. They show the bound is movable, but a cost per accuracy point is not given.

source: Han et al. (2024, v6 2026) Token-budget-aware LLM reasoning (TALE)
finding: Gap 8. Putting a token budget in the prompt shortens the chain, but the chosen budget matters. Below a minimum budget the token cost rises again (token elasticity). Per-question budgets cut cost with a small accuracy loss.
numbers: TALE-EP: output tokens down 67 percent, expense down 59 percent on average, with accuracy 81.03 percent vs 83.75 percent for vanilla CoT (461 tokens) in the one setting I could read. Llama-3.1-8B GSM8K: direct 21.00 percent (38.5 tokens), CoT 77.56 percent (241.5 tokens), TALE-PT-SFT 78.57 percent (139.6 tokens). GSM8K-Zero: CoT 65.04 percent below direct 70.32 percent (overthinking).
quote: if the budget is reduced beyond a certain range, the token cost increases
limits: Budget is in tokens, not a careful/fast instruction. Models up to GPT-4o-mini class. Some table columns are scrambled in the PDF text; only readable rows are quoted.
agent_relevance: An instruction in the prompt can move effective chain length. A budget that is too tight backfires, as an over-low bound does in the diffusion model.

source: Xu, Xie, Zhao, He (2025) Chain of Draft: thinking faster by writing less
finding: Gap 8. Telling the model to keep each step to 5 words matched CoT accuracy on most tasks with far fewer tokens on large models, but not on small models. It is a 'be fast' style instruction with measured accuracy.
numbers: GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet. Date understanding GPT-4o: standard 72.6, CoT 90.2, CoD 88.1 percent. Coin flip: standard 73.2 (GPT-4o) and 85.2 (Claude); CoT and CoD both 100 percent. Sports on Claude: tokens 189.4 to 14.3 (-92.4 percent). CoD uses as little as 7.6 percent of CoT tokens. Models under 3B: gap to CoT larger.
limits: A change of reasoning style, not a change of bound. GSM8K table text scrambled so not quoted. Two frontier models of 2024.
agent_relevance: A prompt instruction can cut tokens up to 10x on easy tasks at 0 to 2 points of accuracy; supports a cheap fast mode for easy items. It does not test the diffusion prediction (bound moves, drift fixed).

source: Jurayj, Cheng, Van Durme (2025) Is that your final answer? Test-time scaling improves selective question answering
finding: Gap 2 and 6. Answering only when confidence passes a threshold raises accuracy of what is answered. More thinking raises confidence in correct answers, but one model (s1-32B) separates wrong from right less well than another (R1-32B). At high thresholds extra compute can lower accuracy of answered items because the extra answered items are less likely correct.
numbers: AIME 2024 and 2025 (60 problems), budgets 500 to 8000 tokens, thresholds 0.0, 0.5, 0.95; R1-32B and s1-32B.
limits: Confidence comes from the model's own answer probability on a forced answer. Math only. 60 problems.
agent_relevance: A confidence bound lets the agent abstain on hard items. Its reliability is model-dependent and must be measured per model.

source: Yue et al. (2024) Large language model cascades with mixture of thought representations
finding: Gap 5 and 2. Using answer agreement of a weak model as the difficulty signal, then escalating to the strong model, cost 40 percent of always using the strong model at equal accuracy. Mixing two prompt styles (chain of thought and program of thought) separated easy from hard questions better than same-prompt samples. This is the only prompt-diversity test found.
numbers: Six reasoning sets, GPT-3.5-turbo weak, GPT-4 strong. Average accuracy 0.929 vs 0.931 for GPT-4 with self-consistency at 40 percent of its cost; CREPE 0.885 vs 0.871 at 47 percent; CoT-2D-Vote 0.924 at 57 percent cost. Threshold swept 0.4 to 1.
quote: can more precisely distinguish between easy and hard reasoning questions
limits: Measures routing quality, not the rate at which agreement is on a wrong answer. 2023-era models. Mixed-prompt gain shown on curves, no single confident-wrong number.
agent_relevance: Varying the prompt between samples is the best-supported way to make agreement more informative; the missing piece is a stated rate of agreed-wrong answers.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Universal self-consistency for large language model generation
finding: Gap 6. For free-form output the model itself can pick the most consistent sample, so agreement works without exact match. It matched standard self-consistency on maths and execution voting on code, and improved summarization and open QA. It gives no confidence level, so a sequential bound cannot be set on it.
numbers: PaLM 2-L: GSM8K SC 90.4 vs USC 90.2; MATH SC 37.9 vs USC 37.4 (as read from the table). BIRD-SQL USC 45.5 vs SC-Exec 45.6. GovReport ROUGE-1 38.8 greedy to 40.2 USC; SummScreen 30.6 to 31.7. USC did not improve GSM8K further at 16 samples vs 8.
limits: Authors state: no confidence estimate, an extra LLM call, sample count bounded by context length, and a notable gap to oracle selection. Fixed N, no stopping.
agent_relevance: For writing and planning, use a selector call over a few drafts, not a vote-share bound. A stop rule there would need a pairwise-agreement estimate that nobody has tested.

source: Vats (2026) Good judgment, bad advice: decision-model controllers raise agent cost without improving success
finding: Gap 7. Re-listed from earlier evidence: the only agent-loop stopping-controller test found. No second controller, model or benchmark was found, but search quota ran out, so this is absence of what I could reach, not proof.
numbers: Terminal-Bench 2.1, 21 tasks, 315 trials: cost per attempt x1.19 (CI 1.02-1.36) at 73.0 percent pass rate.
limits: Only the first page was seen this session (title and abstract).
agent_relevance: Gap 7 stays open. Treat an in-loop controller as unproven and keep a plain cap on steps.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models
finding: Gap 2 and 5. The share of samples agreeing with the final answer is highly correlated with accuracy on GSM8K (stated in the text, plotted in Figure 5), so agreement is a usable difficulty and confidence signal. It is a correlation, not a guarantee.
numbers: Figure 5, GSM8K: agreement share vs accuracy; no per-bin confident-wrong rate given and the plotted values were not extracted.
quote: the consistency is highly correlated with accuracy
limits: 2022 models. Text statement only.
agent_relevance: Justifies first-sample agreement as a cheap difficulty signal. Not evidence for a calibrated bound.

source: Setlur, Rajaraman, Levine, Kumar (2025) Scaling test-time compute without verification or RL is suboptimal
finding: Gap 4. Theory plus experiments with 3B, 8B and 32B models: methods that use a verifier (best-of-N, RL) scale better than methods that imitate good traces, and the gap widens with budget when the base model has varied correct traces.
numbers: Compared S1 distillation with best-of-N using a verifier; the gap grows with test-time budget. No single headline number extracted.
quote: verification is crucial for scaling test-time compute
limits: About training for test-time search, not sequential stopping.
agent_relevance: Backs a verifier signal over an agreement signal when one is available, on principle.

source: Shadlen and Kiani (2013) Decision making as a window on cognition
finding: Gap 9. Bounded evidence integration comes from Wald's sequential probability ratio test: accumulate log likelihood ratio (or a proportional quantity) to a pair of bounds. Flat bounds are optimal only if the evidence-to-logLR conversion is known or the evidence is stationary; with unknown reliability or a time cost, bounds should decline. Brains seem to add an urgency signal rather than move the bound.
numbers: No numbers. Monkeys in Yang and Shadlen 2007 weighed cues in units proportional to log likelihood.
quote: There is no reason to assume the bounds are flat.
limits: A 2013 Neuron review by the same lab, standing in for Gold and Shadlen 2007 (paywalled, not opened).
agent_relevance: Confirms our SPRT reading, and says a Beta/SPRT bound is optimal only when per-sample reliability is known and stationary. With mixed difficulty it should decline or be capped.

source: Ratcliff and McKoon (2008) The diffusion decision model: theory and data for two-choice decision tasks
finding: Gap 9. In the diffusion model the boundary a is a distance in accumulated-evidence units, with drift v, starting point z and noise. It is not a log likelihood ratio by definition. The authors say current diffusion analyses do not explain how criteria are set, and that people set them from verbal instructions on the first trial.
numbers: Parameters: boundary separation a, starting point z, drift v, non-decision time. Errors are slower than correct when accuracy is stressed, faster when speed is stressed.
quote: no current account can explain how human subjects set or calibrate criteria
limits: Stands in for Ratcliff 1978 (not opened). The quote is trimmed from a longer sentence.
agent_relevance: The DDM bound and an LLR bound are different objects; only likelihood-based models link them. Our Beta posterior reading is a Bayesian choice, not what Ratcliff 1978 defined. Instruction-based criterion setting is shown in humans only.

source: Gold and Shadlen (2007) The neural basis of decision making (metadata only)
finding: Gap 9. Full text is not open access (Europe PMC: not in PMC, 2,729 citations). Only bibliographic data was seen; content claims about the SPRT reading come from d18.
numbers: Annu Rev Neurosci 30:535-574; PMID 17600525.
limits: Not opened; cite for existence only.
agent_relevance: Use d18 for citations until the full text is read.
